observation.visible_scene: A long-legged wading bird (heron) is seen from behind, standing in a shallow, calm tidal channel with its neck stretched straight upward in an alert posture. Its pale, sunlit back and the vertical column of its neck are mirrored by a wavering reflection directly below it in the water. The channel runs diagonally across the frame, bordered by dark, wet mud/sand flats above and below. At the far left edge a second, pale bird is intermittently visible. Low-angle light gives warm highlights on the bird's plumage.
visible_changes: The central heron holds its upright, neck-extended stance for the whole excerpt; its body position relative to the water and mud boundaries stays essentially fixed.
Over the sequence the head/neck tilts very slightly backward (the top of the neck drifts a few pixels to one side relative to the body), but no strike, step, or flight occurs.
The reflection beneath the heron continuously shimmers and elongates as small surface ripples move, while the bird itself does not translate.

A pale bird at the left frame edge gradually becomes more visible (a white head/body sliver appears around the middle frames) and then recedes toward the edge again, indicating it drifted relative to the frame rather than the central heron moving.

The background mud-flat pattern and the bird's position shift by a small amount frame-to-frame, consistent with a slight handheld/camera drift, but the magnitude is minor and the scene is otherwise static.
outside_clip_unknowns: Whether the heron's neck-extended posture precedes or follows a hunting strike (prey capture) is not shown.
The full identity, activity, and position of the left-edge bird are unknown because it is mostly outside the frame.
Whether the slight apparent drift is camera movement or actual bird movement cannot be resolved from this segment alone.
uncertain_details: The tiny backward tilt of the neck is subtle and could be partly camera shake rather than a deliberate posture change.
The small overall shift of the scene between first and last frames may be camera drift; background texture changes are too slight to confirm direction.
The left-edge pale shape is too cropped to identify as a separate bird versus an object with certainty.
